It borrows services from a request that has already ended, its exceptions go nowhere, and a shutdown doesn't wait for it. Queue the data instead and let a hosted service do the work in its own scope, and use a durable queue when the work must survive a restart.

When a deploy stops the app, the host signals its

and waits for them to finish, up to a 30-second default timeout. Then the process exits. A task that isn't part of any hosted service just stops wherever it is. In a test, a three-second "send" started half a second before shutdown never completed and left no log line. The same work running in a hosted service kept the host alive until it finished.
Every request starts another task on the same pool that serves requests. A traffic spike becomes a spike of background work with nothing to slow it down, competing with the requests themselves.

content.text: Items still waiting in the channel vanish when the process stops, and a crash may skip the graceful shutdown entirely. For work you can't afford to lose, such as payments or legal notices, store the job in the database in the same transaction as the order, and let the worker process it and mark it done.
